title: Mobile API Design & Backend-for-Frontend
summary: Shaping APIs for mobile's specific constraints — payload size, chattiness, versioning against clients you can't force-update — and the Backend-for-Frontend pattern that aggregates multiple services for one screen.

slides.markdown: A web dashboard on a fast, reliable connection and a phone on patchy cellular data with a battery to protect are different clients with different real constraints, even calling the 'same' backend — and an API designed only with the dashboard in mind tends to punish the mobile client specifically. General API-design theory (REST/GraphQL/gRPC trade-offs, versioning strategy, pagination) lives in [System Design](caching-fundamentals); this topic is the mobile-specific application: what changes when the client is a phone, and the **Backend-for-Frontend** pattern that lets a mobile team shape its own API surface without waiting on every downstream service team.

slides.sectionTitle: Why mobile needs a different API shape
slides.markdown:
Three constraints a web dashboard mostly doesn't have to the same degree:

- **Metered, variable bandwidth** — a payload that's a rounding error on broadband is real, felt latency and real data cost on cellular, and the connection quality itself varies moment to moment.
- **Battery cost of radio usage** — every network request wakes the radio, which costs real battery; five small chatty requests cost more battery than one larger one, not less, even at the same total byte count.
- **A client you can't force-update** — a web app's users get the latest JS on next page load; a percentage of mobile users are always running an app version from months or years ago, because they haven't updated, and an API change has to keep serving them.

Every mobile-specific API practice in this topic is a direct response to one of these three constraints.

slides.subTitle: sending only what the screen needs
slides.markdown:
A general-purpose `/users/{id}` endpoint returning every field a `User` object has — bio, settings, internal flags, admin metadata — is fine for a web dashboard's user-management page and wasteful for a mobile profile header that shows a name and an avatar. **Payload shaping** means the API (often via the BFF layer) returns exactly what a specific screen needs, not a generic full-resource representation every consumer has to filter client-side.

GraphQL's field-selection model solves this natively — the client asks for exactly the fields it wants. A REST-based BFF achieves the same effect by defining screen-specific endpoints (`/mobile/profile-header` returning just name and avatar URL) rather than one generic resource endpoint every client filters down from. Either way, the underlying discipline is the same: don't make the mobile client download and discard data it never renders.

slides.subTitle: for infinite-scroll screens
slides.markdown:
Cursor-based pagination ("give me the next page after cursor X") is generally the right default for mobile infinite-scroll feeds over offset-based pagination ("give me records 100-120") — offset pagination breaks in a subtle, hard-to-notice way when the underlying list changes between requests (a new item inserted at the top shifts every subsequent offset, causing skipped or duplicated items on scroll), while a cursor tied to a specific item's position is stable against insertions elsewhere in the list.

**Prefetching** — requesting the next page slightly before the user actually scrolls to the end, once they're within some threshold of it — trades a small amount of possibly-wasted bandwidth (if the user never scrolls further) for eliminating the visible loading-spinner gap at the boundary, which is usually the right trade for a smooth-feeling feed. Both of these are also central to [Caching & Prefetching Strategy for Mobile Clients](caching-prefetching-mobile-clients), which covers the client-side caching layer this pairs with.

| | BFF-per-platform | One general-purpose API |
|---|---|---|
| Payload fit | tailored exactly to each client's actual needs | generic — every client filters what it doesn't need |
| Ownership | mobile team can iterate on its own BFF independently | changes need cross-team coordination across every consumer |
| Duplication risk | some logic can be duplicated across BFFs (iOS BFF, Android BFF, web BFF) | none — one shape, one place |
| Best fit | teams with genuinely different client needs and enough scale to justify separate BFFs | smaller teams/products where one API reasonably serves every client |

A common middle ground: one shared BFF serving both iOS and Android (since their needs are usually much more similar to each other than either is to a web dashboard), rather than three separate BFFs or one API trying to serve everyone. The right granularity depends on how divergent each client's actual needs are, not a fixed rule.

slides.sectionTitle: Versioning an API old clients still call
slides.markdown:
Because a meaningful fraction of users always run an old app version — some indefinitely, if they've disabled auto-updates or the OS version they're on can't run the latest app build — the API has to keep serving them correctly, indefinitely or until a deliberate, communicated sunset.

The practical approach: version the API explicitly (a header or URL path segment, `/v2/...`), never change an existing endpoint's response shape in a way that breaks an old client's parsing (only add fields, never remove or repurpose one an old client reads), and track real version-adoption metrics so you know when it's actually safe to sunset an old version rather than guessing. A hard breaking change without a deprecation window doesn't just annoy stragglers — it can outright break the app for anyone who hasn't updated, which for many products is a non-trivial percentage of the install base at any given time.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a chatty screen making five sequential calls
slides.markdown:
A screen that needs a user's profile, their recent orders, and personalized recommendations, implemented as three (or five, or more) separate sequential API calls made directly from the mobile client, pays the full round-trip latency cost of each one — and on a high-latency cellular connection, that's not additive in a forgiving way; five 200ms round trips genuinely can be a full second of visible loading before the screen is usable.

The fix, precisely, is the BFF pattern from this topic: collapse what the client experiences as one screen's data need into one request, with the aggregation (and any necessary parallelization of the underlying service calls) happening server-side, where the services are close to each other on a fast internal network rather than each one crossing the client's slow, variable mobile connection independently.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a version bump silently breaking old installs
slides.markdown:
Shipping a backend change that renames a field, changes a field's type (a string ID becoming a numeric one), or removes a field an old client's parsing code depends on — without a deprecation window or explicit versioning — can silently break the app for every user still on an old version, sometimes as a hard crash on parse, sometimes as silently missing data that just looks broken.

The practical discipline: treat every API response shape as effectively a public, versioned contract with clients you don't control the update cadence of — additive changes are almost always safe, changes to existing fields almost never are without a new version. Before any breaking change ships, check real version-adoption telemetry for what percentage of active users are still on a version that would break, and if it's non-trivial, that's the signal to add a new versioned endpoint alongside the old one rather than mutating the existing one in place.
